knowledgePoints.name: Three paths after writing a prompt
knowledgePoints.teach:
There are exactly three things people do once a prompt seems to work.

  1. Test once, ship it. High risk: real input is stranger than anything you invented.
  2. Test a few times, patch a corner case or two. Better. Users will still surprise you.
  3. Run it through an evaluation pipeline, score it, iterate on objective metrics. More upfront work and cost, much higher confidence.

Most engineers default to 1 and 2, and underestimate real-world edge cases.

Worth being precise about what “it works on the three cases I tried” establishes: that the prompt fails on none of three cases you thought of. It says nothing about the cases you did not think of, which is the entire population you are about to serve.

The distinction underneath all this: prompt engineering is techniques for writing better prompts. Prompt evaluation is measuring whether they worked.

questions.q: What does passing the handful of cases you invented actually establish?
options: That the prompt is ready for typical input
Only that it survives the cases you imagined
That the remaining failure rate is under 5%
That it generalises, the cases being typical
questions.explain: Cases you invented are drawn from your imagination, not from production traffic. They cannot speak for what you did not imagine.

questions.q: How do prompt engineering and prompt evaluation differ?
options: Engineering is manual, evaluation automated
Engineering is pre-deploy, evaluation is after
Engineering writes prompts; evaluation measures
Engineering is for system, evaluation for user
questions.explain: One writes, the other measures. The cycle alternates between them.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the stated cost of the third path?
options: More upfront work and cost, for confidence
It requires a much more capable model
It cannot handle prompts with examples
It only works for classification tasks
reviewQuestions.explain: The trade is explicit: effort and spend now, confidence later.

knowledgePoints.name: Five steps
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Draft a prompt — the baseline.
  2. Create an eval dataset — sample inputs representative of production traffic.
  3. Feed through Claude — merge each input into the prompt template, collect outputs.
  4. Feed through a grader — score each output, typically 1–10.
  5. Change the prompt and repeat — compare average scores.

Step 2 happens once. Steps 3 to 5 run again on every iteration.

That asymmetry is what turns the dataset into a regression suite: because the same inputs are re-scored after every change, a technique that fixes one case and breaks two others shows up as a lower average rather than as a success story.

questions.q: Which artefact persists across iterations rather than being rebuilt?
options: The prompt you are refining
The grader's own reasoning
The score threshold you set
The dataset of test cases
questions.explain: The dataset is built once and reused, which is what makes it a regression suite.

questions.q: What does re-scoring the same dataset after every prompt change catch?
options: A change fixing one case, breaking others
Rate-limit errors during a long run
Drift in the underlying model itself
Cases missing from the dataset entirely
questions.explain: Regression. Without a fixed dataset, a net-negative change can look like a win.

reviewQuestions.q: Put the pipeline in order: grade, draft, run through Claude, build dataset, revise.
options: build dataset → draft → grade → run through Claude → revise
draft → run through Claude → build dataset → grade → revise
draft → build dataset → run through Claude → grade → revise
build dataset → run through Claude → draft → grade → revise
reviewQuestions.explain: Draft, dataset, run, grade, revise — then loop back to the run.

reviewQuestions.q: What score range does the course use for graders?
options: Pass/fail
A letter grade

knowledgePoints.name: Generate it cheaply, keep it small at first
knowledgePoints.teach:
Datasets can be hand-written, but generating them is normal — and the model that generates is not the model under test.

Use Haiku to generate. The dataset is not the thing being evaluated, so it does not need the expensive tier.

Generate with prefill plus stop sequences so the result parses cleanly: prefill the assistant turn with ```json, set stop_sequences=["```"], then json.loads.

On size: keep it to two or three cases while you are actively iterating, so a run is fast and cheap enough that you actually do it. Scale up to tens or hundreds for final validation. Real production datasets run to hundreds or thousands of records.

questions.q: Which model generates the eval dataset for a Sonnet prompt, and why?
options: Sonnet, so cases match the model under test
Haiku — generating cases is not the task
Opus, since case quality drives eval quality
The same model, to avoid any mismatch
questions.explain: Generation is a separate, cheap task. Applying the cheapest-model rule here is the point.

questions.q: How large should the dataset be during active prompt iteration?
options: Hundreds, so every change is measured well
Exactly 20–30, as for the model selection
As large as the rate limit will let you go
Two or three cases, so iteration stays fast
questions.explain: Small while iterating, large to validate. A slow eval is an eval that gets skipped.

knowledgePoints.name: The format field
knowledgePoints.teach:
Give each test case a format field — "python", "json", "regex":

{
  "input": "Match any UK postcode",
  "format": "regex"      ← tells the grader which validator to run
}

A code grader has several validators available — json.loads, ast.parse, re.compile — and no way to guess which one applies to a given output. The field is how the dataset tells it.

Without it, a mixed dataset either needs one grader per format (and a way to split the cases) or a grader that tries everything and cannot distinguish 'not valid Python' from 'not Python at all'.

questions.q: What is the per-case `format` field for?
options: Telling the code grader which validator
Telling Claude which format to produce
Recording which model produced the case
Selecting a temperature for each case
questions.explain: It routes the output to the right validator — json.loads, ast.parse, re.compile.

questions.q: Which three validators does the course name for code grading?
options: json.loads, ast.parse, re.compile
pydantic, mypy, and black
jsonschema, pytest, flake8
eval, exec, and compile
questions.explain: One per format: JSON, Python, regular expression.

reviewQuestions.q: Why generate a dataset with prefill and stop sequences rather than plain prompting?
options: It is noticeably cheaper per token used
It is the only way to get more than three
It guarantees the cases are representative
It yields JSON clean enough to just parse
reviewQuestions.explain: Clean parsing. The technique is the structured-output one, applied to a generation task.

knowledgePoints.name: Objective, instant, and blind
knowledgePoints.teach:
A code grader is a programmatic check. It handles anything with a right answer a computer can verify:

  • length,
  • keyword presence or absence,
  • syntax validity — JSON, Python, regex,
  • readability scores.
def syntax_score(output, fmt):
    try:
        {"json": json.loads, "python": ast.parse, "regex": re.compile}[fmt](output)
        return 10
    except Exception:
        return 0

Note the shape: try/except, 10 on success, 0 on failure. It is deliberately binary, because syntax is binary.

A code grader can tell you the output parses. It cannot tell you the output is any good.

One useful adjunct: improve format compliance by pre-filling the response with a code-block opener, forcing raw code and nothing else.

questions.q: Which property can a code grader check?
options: Whether the answer is genuinely helpful
Whether the reasoning behind it is sound
Whether the output parses as valid JSON
Whether the tone suits its intended audience
questions.explain: Syntax validity is exactly its brief. The other three need a model or a human.

questions.q: Why is a syntax code grader scored 10 or 0 rather than on a scale?
options: To make averaging with a model score easy
The scale is reserved for model graders
To penalise malformed output more heavily
Syntax parses or it does not; no middle

reviewQuestions.q: An output is beautifully argued and does not parse. What does a code grader give it?
options: A middling score
It skips the case
reviewQuestions.explain: 0. The grader sees the parse failure and nothing else — which is precisely why you combine it with a model score.

knowledgePoints.name: Ask for reasoning, not a number
knowledgePoints.teach:
A model grader is a second Claude call that scores the first one's output — for quality, instruction-following, completeness, helpfulness, safety. Things no try/except can reach.

There is one failure mode that catches everybody:

Ask a model for a bare score and it returns about 6 out of 10, regardless of actual quality.

The fix is to ask for the reasoning as well as the number:

Evaluate the response below.

Return:
  strengths:   what it does well
  weaknesses:  where it falls short
  reasoning:   how you weighed those against the criteria
  score:       1-10

Storing the reasoning alongside the score is not just for auditing. It is what makes the score real: a model that has to justify a 9 will not award one to a mediocre answer, and a flat distribution of 6s is a symptom you can now see the cause of.

questions.q: Every output in your eval scores between 5 and 7. What is most likely wrong?
options: The dataset is too small to separate them
The graded model's temperature is too low
The outputs genuinely are all mediocre
The grading prompt asks for a bare score
questions.explain: A flat band around 6 is the documented signature of a grader asked for a number and nothing else.

questions.q: What should a model grader be asked to return?
options: A score only, for consistency's sake
Strengths, weaknesses, reasoning, score
A pass/fail verdict plus a rewrite
A score and its confidence interval
questions.explain: All four. The reasoning is what stops the score collapsing to the middle.

reviewQuestions.q: What should be stored per test case from a model grader?
options: The score and the reasoning
The score, and nothing else
The graded output and the score
The score and the grader's model id
reviewQuestions.explain: Score plus reasoning, averaged across the dataset — the reasoning is what tells you where a prompt is failing.

reviewQuestions.q: Which qualities is a model grader suited to judging?
options: Quality, instruction-following, safety
Syntax validity and output length
Token cost and end-to-end latency
Schema conformance of the output
reviewQuestions.explain: The judgement calls. Anything mechanically checkable belongs to the code grader, which is cheaper and never wrong.

knowledgePoints.name: Three graders, and the combination
knowledgePoints.teach:
graderhowbest at
Codeprogrammatic checkslength, keywords, syntax validity, readability
Modelanother Claude callquality, instruction-following, completeness, safety
Humanmanual reviewnuance, comprehensiveness, depth, relevance — most flexible, slowest

In practice you combine the first two:

final = (model_score + syntax_score) / 2

An eloquent answer that does not parse now scores 5, not 10 — and a parseable answer that says nothing scores 5, not 10.

Each grader's blind spot is the other's specialty, which is the whole reason to average them rather than pick one.

questions.q: Outputs must be valid Python and must actually solve the problem. How do you grade that?
options: A model grader, since it can read code
A human grader; both criteria are subjective
A code grader with a much stricter validator
Code for syntax, model for quality, averaged
questions.explain: Two criteria of different kinds, so two graders — combined, e.g. (model_score + syntax_score) / 2.

questions.q: What is the human grader's stated trade-off?
options: Cheapest but also the least accurate
The fastest option for large datasets
Most flexible on nuance, but very slow
Only usable for a final safety review
questions.explain: Flexibility at the cost of throughput, which is why it is reserved for nuance.

reviewQuestions.q: Why average a code score with a model score rather than using whichever is lower?
options: Averaging is simply cheaper to compute
Each grader's blind spot is the other's
The minimum would always be the code score
Averaging keeps every score inside 1–10
reviewQuestions.explain: You are measuring two different things and want both represented, not the worse of them.
